utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before we start working, I have an objection. You know full well that I was not here last week, although I had wanted to do otherwise, and I wish to draw your attention to the following: Article 21 of your Statute, paragraph 4. You know that very well. It refers to the minimum guarantees, entitled to the following minimum guarantees. I am quoting (D) from your Statute: To be present. Cross-examination is part of regular proceedings, so I think that my rights have been infringed upon if an attempt is made to have this done in my absence. I also wish to draw your attention to Article 14(D), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the same is set out there as a minimum guaranteed right. So these are parts of jus cogens, cogent rights, so there are no exceptions whatsoever which would allow you to decide to continue proceedings in my absence. Therefore, I raise this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber considered this matter, gave a ruling on it, considered that in the circumstances it was appropriate. If you have an objection and you wish to insist on it, you can take the matter elsewhere. Mr. Nice, please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, the accused served a purpose by becoming leader of your group in 1980 -- I say by becoming leader of your group but by becoming a leader who espoused the interests of your group in 1986, didn't he? 1987.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He then used your group to achieve his own objectives, in particular the centralisation of Serbia through bringing about the downfall of Montenegro and Vojvodina's leadership, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He then dropped you as you'd ceased to be of use to him.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice and gentlemen of the Trial Chamber, I was never in power, before Milosevic or after Milosevic. I was never on the police force. I was never a spy. I did not participate in the war. I don't see how I could have been in any kind of authority, so how could anybody have dropped me when I wasn't there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that my time is limited. The accused remained vulnerable to the pressure of nationalist Serbs like you right through to the end of the 1990s, as you made clear in the middle of the 1990s, in 1994. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in the 19 -- in 1994 -- we're going to come back and look at the terms of your 1985 petition which have now been translated into English, but for time reasons I'm going to go straight to 1994. You were the first signatory on another petition, and this petition shows the linkage between national Serbs, Kosovo, and the other wars with which this -- in respect of which this accused is charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the document please be distributed. We've looked at it earlier, Your Honours, but -- I think, but we haven't seen it in this final version which has the translation associated with the document itself. The document as photocopied in the version we have doesn't start with signatory number one but I think Mr. Bulatovic will confirm that he was signatory number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, time doesn't allow me but to go through a few of the paragraphs of this petition. We can see it summarised elsewhere. And on the third paragraph, the petition says: "The current Serbian authorities which were given an historic chance as well as an historic obligation and responsibility to seriously resolve one of the biggest problems of the Serbian nation have been bypassing Kosmet for the fourth year." Next paragraph: "The Serbian issue in Kosovo and Metohija has become a means of winning and preserving power while the Serbian people in Kosovo have been portrayed as a militant and stormy element unworthy of anyone's sacrifice for their salvation. Because of such a picture the Serbian issue in Kosovo has become a burden to the authorities and the opposition which everybody now is avoiding." If you go on, please, to the next paragraph but two, I think, and on the Court's page it's the start of the next sheet, beginning, "Due to ill defined and inconsistent Serbian policy..." but the sixth line says this: "In March 1995, it will be five years since the passing of the programme of Serbian colonisation of Kosmet which promised the settlement of a hundred thousand Serbs. Unfortunately, not only were only a negligible number settled there but the exodus continued while at the same time more than 25.000 new Albanians were born." And in the demands, the numbered nine demands, number 2 seeks halting of the process of Albanisation; number 4, that the parallel ethnic state be crushed; and number 7, that there be colonisation of Kosovo. Now, that's a petition that you were the first signatory of in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not a signatory. I'm not the first signatory. Now, did I sign it at all, that is something I cannot claim. I cannot see my signature here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you had a point to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to go into the interpretation, Mr. Robinson, but the Serb colonisation of Kosovo is not mentioned anywhere in the Serbian version of this text, whereas Mr. Nice referred to it twice, the Serb colonisation of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's in the English text. Can we have another translation of the B/C/S? It's number 7. Can we have the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Settling Kosovo. "To urgently adopt a programme of the settlement of Kosovo and to ensure money for its implementation." No colonisation of Kosovo is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now please look at the next document which I'd like you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I just want to thank Mr. Milosevic for that clarification, because "colonisation" is a loaded word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at a newspaper article of the 21st of October of 1994. If you'd like to look at this newspaper article, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber may like to look at the original first to see the photograph and the set-out of this document. It's headed "Milosevic has betrayed us." Can the witness have the version, please, opened at the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, again I got the very same article that Mr. Nice presented a few moments ago, and he is referring to a different article now, but I got the same one yet again, just a different copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you ensure that the accused has the correct version, correct article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see the -- can I have a look at the article he's got there? This article is headed "Milosevic has betrayed us." It has a picture of you. It's dated the 21st of October of 1994, and I'm going to read a few passages from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have just been given now, Mr. Nice, the correct article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry there was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The English translation of the article on the first page says this of you, Mr. Bulatovic, in the middle of the page in English: "No individual is better qualified to testify to the dissatisfaction of Kosovar Serbs, to outline the reasons for the reactivation of the resistance movement, and to organise a new petition than Bulatovic, and he has again been the first to sign it." And then three paragraphs further on, it says this as your observation in the interview: "Our petition was also motivated by that fear. It simply awoke us from a deep sleep. If Milosevic renounces the Srpska republic overnight, where he has people and territory, what will happen with this part of Serbia, where he has neither people nor territory? There are fewer than 200.000 Serbs in Kosovo, which is in ethnic Albanian hands." Your next answer says: "Of course it is our joint struggle, and whether we shall succeed in defending the territory of the Serbian people across the Drina is precisely the issue on which depends our strength to defend Serbian interests here as well." And you go on, Mr. Bulatovic, in the interview record to say this: "Second, since it is we Serbs from Kosovo who created Milosevic and let his genie out of the bottle, we consider ourselves to be responsible for everything that is happening to the Serbian people and Serbia today. Milosevic soared to the throne on the shoulder of the Serbian Resistance Movement in Kosovo and Metohija. The movement prepared everything for him and enabled him to rule in whatever way pleases him." The interviewer asked you: "You seem to be disappointed with the President of Serbia," to which you replied: "God could not have laid a greater misfortune upon our Serbs than to leave the communists in the power, instead of [Joseph Tito] Broz to give us a little Broz." You were asked: "Still, the fact is that you supported Milosevic and stood by his side," to which you replied this: "That is not true. Milosevic stood by my side as long as he needed me and the entire resistance movement. The movement was established in 1981, it became stronger until 1986, when Milosevic came to Kosovo Polje in April 1987 and simply captured our hearts with the famous statement of his, that nobody will be allowed to beat us Serbs. He needed us until early 1989 when he formed the Red Peony ... and ideologically coloured the national question." Do you accept everything you said in that interview, Mr. Bulatovic, as accurate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly yes, partly no. We accepted the words that President Milosevic had said at the gathering in Kosovo Polje, and this morning at 6.30 a.m., it is exactly 19 years since that event, precisely this morning. He spoke to us then like any other politician from Belgrade who came to see us. We did not agree with Milosevic's predecessors either, or with their positions. They left Kosovo, and they practically sold us down the river, the leadership of Serbia did. We wanted to voice our criticism in view of him and in view of his predecessors so that the voice of Serbs there would be heard so that we would be finally brought to an equal position to the Siptars and the others in Kosovo and Metohija. It's not that we created Milosevic or that he created us. It is our own trouble that created us, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if you didn't speak at the same time. Mr. Nice, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, not for the first time you've used the word "Siptars" about Kosovo Albanians. You know that the word "Siptar" on the mouth of a Serb is offensive.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why do you use it in this Court?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's nothing offensive about it. The Siptars, they call their own country Sipu. Maybe you don't know that. It's not offensive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be offensive if I call them Arnauts, like the Turks called them, but saying "Siptar," there's nothing wrong with that. That is their national state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, it is --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- offensive to Albanians to call them Siptars if you are a non-Albanian, and you know that. And believe me, there are Albanians here in this room. Would you be so good as to describe them in a less offensive way.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad if there are Albanians here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the Court can understand the Prosecution's position on this - we've heard earlier evidence on it - there can be terms such as, for example, Polak. My suggestion to this witness is that it is as offensive to use the word Siptars by a Serb as it would be for non-Poles to use the word Polaks to and about Polish people although that is itself a Polish term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Mr. Milosevic did ask the question of -- to the witness, and he answered that it is the way that themselves described themselves. But I understand your point. It is that for a non-Albanian to use the term it is offensive to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. And there are Albanians and Albanian speakers in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I take you now, please, Mr. Bulatovic, for want of time, to two more passages in this interview of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are we so far? I mean, I have divined nothing from the question and answer -- the way the question was posed, Mr. Nice, inevitably produced the answer which came, and really has advanced matters not at all, as far as I can see, unless you can guide me to something that I ought to have taken from that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly can. Your Honour should see from this document that this man out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, from his answer, not from the document. I'm trying to understand -- I don't know what he accepts and what he doesn't at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem with that is that he gave a long answer which was non-responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Partly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about that. The question inevitably drew the answer, I think, that it got that part of it he accepts and part he doesn't, but I have no idea which part he accepts and which part he doesn't accept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- nail points down, and the Court knows what time restraint I will be under if I accommodate the two-thirds protocol. What I was hoping to do, because the answer was long and non-specific, was to put the two other passages to the witness and ask him to accept the two points that I want from him, but that's all I can do in the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Nice, but first of all, the witness denied his signature at the letter but the first passage in this document says Mr. Bulatovic the signatory, signatory to the letter. We could pursue that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to pursue that again at the end, but I can pursue it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, in this interview you're identified as the first signatory of the letter. Is that correct? Were you the first signatory? The photocopy we have starts at number 6, I believe.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that I cannot remember any of this. As for the petition of the 2,016, yes, I was the first to sign, and 219 of the wisest person -- people in the Serb nation supported it, and I said that the first day here before the Trial Chamber, and I don't think that can be contested in any way. Now, when we come to this, the criticisms of Mr. Milosevic, this is just proof of the fact that we Serbs were not satisfied with the fact that no steps were taken in Kosovo and Metohija after he came to visit Kosovo Polje, and you're attacking him and saying that he did lots of things there against - how shall I put this? - against the Albanians - you want me to call them Albanians; is that right? - to fulfil our will. So if that doesn't -- anyway, we Serbs call the Albanians who came to Kosovo from Albanian, Mr. Robinson. That's who we refer to as Albanians. But those who were born there and were there all the time, we refer to them as the Siptars. We Serbs do, I mean. To clarify that issue. So I don't think that I insulted them in any way. Now, whether you believe me or not is up to you, but you're the first person that has made that remark in the past 60 years and I've been living there for 62 years. No Albanian ever told me anything like that. You don't have to believe me, but that's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at two more passages in this interview and I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. If the Chamber on its second sheet would go three-quarters of the way down and if you turn on a -- no, first of all we have to -- let's deal with this. In the middle of the second page you -- dealing with the organisation the Red Peony, you said: "... solely for that reason: to square accounts with the leaders of the resistance movement, to pronounce them traitors and turn the national platform into a platform of the communist party. Milosevic was afraid of the leadership of the resistance movement and knew that I was an implacable anti-communist. Since I knew that, if I did not stop, a car might hit me, or a brick from some dilapidated house might fall on my head ..." Quick observation there: You're describing there the sort of violence that might come to those who disagree with authority, are you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the situation is like today in Serbia, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Worse things are happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was then under the accused?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. I'll give you a very clear answer to that question straight away: This text is a criticism for us to force the president, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, to take radical steps in Kosovo and Metohija. He didn't take any steps. And on the other hand, you're accepting this that in relation to the authorities was provocative. That's true, it was provocative in order that something should be done, that the authorities should do something, because they didn't take any steps. Nothing was done. The republican authorities in Belgrade were worse than in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on to --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we expected them to give us protection and they didn't protect us, so that's where the crux of the matter lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next answer but two, I think: "The fact that he hasn't changed the political system but is rather trying to settle problems by using the old power mechanism is our greatest disappointment. He has remained a communist, which is best seen in the fact that his party's interests are more important to him than national interests. He wants to settle the Serbian national question and to preserve communism at the same time. He gave up the national struggle for the Serbian territories across the Drina for ideological reasons. Fearing that the epidemic from there might spread over here, he has imposed more severe sanctions against the Srpska republic than the UN Security Council did against Yugoslavia." Now, pausing there, you didn't know, did you, from your position, the degree of daily support that the accused was actually providing for those across the Drina despite the appearance of a blockade, did you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know at all that Serbia was becoming involved, and we considered that it should become involved because that's where our people were. And you couldn't leave your people to be slaughtered as in World War II. You have to protect it. And that border on the Drina was intercepted. And all links were cut off with the republic. So this was a criticism of those positions and that policy. And on the other hand, you attack Mr. Milosevic, our president, and say that he interfered across the Drina River. We're criticising him for not having interfered to protect the people. We were left Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unprotected. Those across the Drina were left unprotected. So it was the same when lions are attacking you. When lions attack herds of cattle in the desert and they devour them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you just wait a minute, please. I want to consult with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure how this line of cross-examination supports your case. It seems to be the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will in part have to wait for my next question and in part have to await arguments built on the rest of the evidence, but the Court will remember, it has heard it already elsewhere, there is evidence that flowed -- that aid was flowing daily, from the mouth of the accused himself, despite the blockade. In any event, putting in a document like this for the purpose I'm going to put it in, requires to be put in, broadly speaking, in full, both sides. Now to my question to the witness, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, Mr. Bulatovic, were concerned on behalf of nationalist Serbs to put this accused under pressure because he wasn't doing enough, so you said, either for the Kosovo Serbs or for the Serbs across the Drina, and he reacted to your demands and gave you what he wanted -- what you wanted, didn't he, in two ways.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, why, having been quite so critical, and the Chamber can see the rest of the highly critical terms you addressed to the accused, can you explain why you're now such a supporter of his if he didn't respond to you and give you what you wanted?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we -- we weren't given what we wanted but he did do a part of it, and this is what he did: The constitution of Serbia and the provinces was changed, was amended. The provinces had more power than Serbia proper, Central Serbia. And with the amendments in the constitution, those provinces came under the authority of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that part of the job was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're now in 1994. What --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely because nothing was undertaken against -- to combat terror and terrorism in Kosovo. Terrorism in Kosovo prevailed and the authorities from Serbia - and Serbia now had absolute power - did nothing radical, took no radical steps there. There was so much killing there, and you have facts and figures, you delve in politics yourself. I'm sure you have information, as a prosecutor, of the number of people --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... get an answer and then I'm going to suggest to you what the answer is if you don't tell me. What is it, please, that this accused did between 1994 and today that makes you such a supporter of his given your criticism in 1994? Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, certainly, certainly. It's very simple, Mr. Nice, a very simple answer. We demanded of him you know what, it's written down in the text, you have it in front you. Not in that interview, I mean, but generally our demands, our requests, and the constitutional amendments went through. But radical steps for us to have life in security and safety, that we could move around properly, that we could work normally, that we could take part in the life of Kosovo and Metohija, that's what we didn't have and that's what we asked for, so from that time we expressed our dissatisfaction about that. I don't know if I've explained this properly. Now, why am I defending him today? Because the indictment is false. That's why I'm defending him. Because had he taken any steps in Kosovo, had he done anything radical there, what kind of indictment would you have had then? If we were brought into a position of equality, whereas people had to leave their universities, their schools, their companies, there was public sabotage by the Albanians, and the authorities, the powers that be knew about this and did nothing about it, did nothing to help us. So that's where the conflict lies. And the whole nation today in Serbia, I'm sure you have your intelligence services and know about all that, but all the people in Serbia were surprised as to who wrote the indictment. Not even if Pristina had written the indictment would it have been worded in the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand that my general proposition to you is that this accused, although he dropped you in 1988 and 1989, remained vulnerable to the pressure of nationalist Serbs, and following this petition and your letter, the -- even the appearance of the blockade against the Serbs in the Drina diminished towards the end of 1994. That's one way in which he met your demands. But the other way in which he met your demands and satisfied you was to start the process of attacking in an institutional way the Kosovo Albanians. And that started in 1995, and it was responsive in part or whole to your pressure, and that's one of the reasons you support him, isn't it, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. First of all, it's not correct that he rejected us. And who are we? You have the whole nation, all the people there. I wasn't there alone. So I was interested in whether I could survive with my family in Kosovo and Metohija and continue living there. Not my family but every Serb family in Kosovo and Metohija. And that is what you, Mr. Nice, do not wish or cannot understand or do not wish to understand, I don't know which, and that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me give you a few examples. You remember the famous 200 police trial where Kosovo Albanian policemen were tried and subject to heavy sentences. That was responsive to this pressure of yours, and it was said at the time by human rights organisations to be responsive to this sort of pressure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year was that, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the same time, human rights organisations in 1995 were recording the increase in oppression of Kosovo Albanians by discrimination in employment, by police brutality, by restrictions on freedom of association, and by political trials. That was responsive to your pressure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were a --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your reports aren't correct. Your information is not correct. There was no pressure exerted on them. What happened was that at that time, and we didn't know who they were contacting, which forces in the world were supporting them, that's what we didn't know, so that they could go about doing the underhand things they did. So we had a state, whereas they did not have a state of their own and what they wanted was a state of their own. So everything that what -- were belonged to the state was sabotaged and their behaviour to it was that they should destroy it, destroy everything that was the state. That was the difference between their population and our population. And according to what I know today, that's it. I didn't know all that then. I must say that loud and clear before this Tribunal. I've come here to tell the truth, not to tell stories and tales of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as we move on to other events of the late 1990s before I return to the 1980s for the time that I may, to show the continued integration of your pressure and of Kosovo and the other conflict areas, do you remember in 1996, in July of 1996, a full year after Srebrenica, being interviewed on the British Broadcasting Corporation, praising Radovan Karadzic as the most popular living Serb, pressing for him to be president of the joint country of Serbia and Montenegro? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was -- is that still your view, that Radovan Karadzic is the greatest living Serb, most popular living Serb?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- have not a moment's hesitation about any of the things that happened in the course of his leadership in Bosnia, do you? Not a moment's hesitation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean "moment's hesitation"? He stood at the head of the people to save the people, not to suffer the same fate as they did in World War II at Jasenovac and other camps, and he did what he could to save them. A lot of people did die. A war is a war. So Karadzic did for his people as best he could to protect them. What he was able to protect, he did protect. What he didn't, it was God's fate and destiny that that happened. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last thing that the accused did that makes you so favourable to him now, Mr. Bulatovic, is that he, following March 1999, had hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians kicked out and thousands killed, didn't he? And that met your national Serb demands.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your observations. That's not true. I'll tell you this: I was in hospital when the shelling in Kosovo started and the NATO pact aggression on Yugoslavia started. I found myself in hospital undergoing treatment. And let me tell you straight away that from Kosovo everybody fled who was able to flee, both the Serbs and the Siptars -- I mean Albanians, if you want - all right, I'll say Albanians now -- and the Roma and the Macedonians and the Turks around Prizren, which is where they mostly lived, everybody tried to escape from the territory that was being shelled, to take refuge. Now, imagine this: Had the people not fled outside the territory that was rocketed, that was shelled, can you imagine how many more thousands would have lost their lives? Nobody expelled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bulatovic. That's not responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody expelled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidence in this Court may satisfy the learned Judges in due course that thousands were killed and hundreds of thousands expelled by Serbs. You know that to be the case, don't you, and that's why you approve of this accused, and that's why you're here to help him.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know about those thousands killed. In our country, the figures say that 2 or 3.000 Albanians were killed and as many Serbs, roughly, about 2.000 Serbs, a little less Serbs than Albanians. Therefore, all the thousands that you mention and bring up is something that I don't know about, and I'm hearing those figures, those many, many thousands here for the first time today. At Bolija [phoen], for example, now they are extracting the bones of Serbs who were kidnapped and killed, for instance. Now you're skipping over that. There's no word from you about the Serbs as victims, you as the Prosecutor I mean, which means that that is tendentious, sheer tendentiousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may carry on making remarks like that as long as you think it's helping you, but you just tell me this, or tell the learned Judges this: Do you think that the loss of lives in either Bosnia, Croatia, or in Kosovo at the hands of Serbs to the extent that that was proved is justified because of the Serb national interest? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that we should have fought to save our people, and if possible, to save it from genocide. No tendency. I don't think there was any tendency on the part of Karadzic or anybody else that in defending their own people to try and destroy another people. That would mean that ultimately they were working against their own people and were the enemies of their own people. Our views of the world are not the same, Mr. Nice, and I apologise for having to say that. No, they are not. You can't do evil and wish for good. You can only do good and then God will reward you with good, but evil begets evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will look at a 1985 petition which was your -- it had your first signature, because although it was provided, it wasn't provided in English, although it was said to contain no offensive term of any kind in it, so I must use my time to put in the English translation. Because this comes in 1985 -- and let's just remember the position, Mr. Bulatovic: A full ten years before the arrival of what's become known as the KLA, four years only after the demonstrations in Pristina in 1981, four years into your Serb nationalist disappointment with your inability to change the constitution. That's my suggestion to you. And let's see what in fact this mild petition, as it was effectively being described, reveals. You put your signature in 1985 to a petition the second paragraph of which says: "The real situation is crushing. A portion of Yugoslavia is under occupation: the territory of our historical and national entity, while a fascist genocide against us, Kosovo and Metohija Serbs, has gained social recognition." What was the genocide that you were alleging there in public, please.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you're saying that the KLA was created now when the war began, and that's just not true. The KLA was working clandestinely the whole period after the war. But it wasn't as broad based. There were individual killings, cattle were maimed and killed and blinded, roofs were destroyed on houses, for example, and children did that, for instance. So all this type of pressure from the KLA. And it has existed throughout. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is the fascist genocide -- you're writing a document, Mr. Bulatovic. I just want you to understand what I'm asking you about. You're writing a document, distributing it publicly so as to go to your fellow countrymen. Who are you accusing, please, of fascist genocide in 1985?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the Albanian terrorists who waged terrorism throughout Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Nice. And that's what you can't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is 1985. We can look --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, what would you say that it meant if you set fire to the Pec Patriarchy, the very spirit and soul of the Serbian Orthodox Church? What do you think that is? Is it genocide? It is intent, the intent to destroy everything that is Serb in Kosovo and Metohija. They have no cultural movements in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Monuments, I'm sorry, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- monuments in Kosovo and Metohija. Let them tell us what cultural monuments they have and what is the cultural foundation for their being there. They don't have it. They don't have anything to show. Kosovo is the largest Serb cemetery, the largest Serb cemetery and the largest -- most of its churches and monasteries are there and land belonging to Serb monasteries. That is it, Mr. Nice. When you extract somebody's heart, can they continue to live? And that's what the situation like -- is like in Kosovo and Metohija. They want this alien factor to extract the very soul of Serbia. That's how we Serbs see it, and we claim that that is so and it is indeed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're lost in the past, I must suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we done anything against Albanian -- if you want me to say "Albanian," I'll say it -- against the Albanian people, then what would you say then? They terrorised us in our own state. They killed us in our own state and expelled us from our own state or in our own state. Have you got an example anywhere else in the world that you can quote which is similar to that? You are an intelligence man. I am somebody who I'm sure you consider to be illiterate, but can you give me an example in the world of a country which has its own state and allows a minority to come in and terrorise that? That only happened in Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Nice. Rest assured that that is the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... small clip - the audio booth, we're using Sanction - an interview with you. I suggest this reveals, along with your previous answer, where your thinking comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Murat, the man who has that emotion on you, died, what, over 600 years ago?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murat died. He was a Turkish Tsar, leader, and he was killed and so was Knez Lazar, the Serbian leader, at the battle of Kosovo, and that was the only battle in the history of the peoples of the world in which two leaders, Tsars, were killed. There's Lazar on the Serb side and the Turkish Tzar Murat on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few more passages because this document --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- as a document of importance, and what I'm going to suggest to you while we look at it is that the independent human rights reports for the 1980s dealing with Kosovo will show that, yes, there were independent and -- sorry, individual incidents of violence against Kosovo Serbs. Not organised but by individuals, but that was the extent of it. You see? Not a question of organised or KLA or anything like that at the time at which we are concerned. That's my suggestion. We don't have time to go into the reports, but if we look at your petition - I can make them available to the Court, of course - this is what you said. The next paragraph: "Brutal pressure of the Siptar chauvinists..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Judge Kwon has inquired of me whether the video was in fact played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or did we hear anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you didn't hear anything that shouldn't inconvenience the Court because, of course, of the transcript. I don't know whether the soundtrack worked. It should have worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some picture was portrayed in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see a picture with -- or by my question, did Your Honours hear sound?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness says there's no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can put the question built on the video so that there can be no doubt the point I'm making.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You still, Mr. Bulatovic, find an emotional thrill at the contemplation of the last gasp of somebody who was killed 600 years ago, and that's where you are lodged emotionally and, I'm going to suggest, intellectually.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. This footage was taken by the BBC crew, but you should be showing it in extenso, all of it, because I refused to give them an interview because they wouldn't -- they didn't wish to go and conduct the interview to a Serb village but I took them to the Serb village of Crnoljevo, where there's not a single Serb house standing, where there are no -- there's no Serb cemetery. It's all destroyed. And together we put back the grave stones saying who was buried there. And they saw this, the destroyed cemetery. All of this was filmed by the BBC. But it came and went and then produced this programme which is tendentious. And this is what I said, this speech of mine was said at the monument to the Kosovo heroes, so that's where that speech was delivered, at the monument to the Kosovo heroes. And I said that's where the two leaders, the two Tzars were killed, Tzar Lazar and Tzar Murat. Now you seem to just focus on Murat and present an impression to the public as if God knows what had been said there. Everything that was said was honest and decent and honourable at that monument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this petition that you signed in 1985. Go, please, to the demands. You see here under 3 you were pressing for the immediate expulsion of greater Albanian chauvinists who you said were leading a rebellion. 4, to publicly state the names of the genocide project against us. 5, to deny further hospitality to Albanian immigrants. 6, to annul every contract buying or selling Serbian property. And then 11 another hark back, just an example, to reconstruct the personal files of the Albanian Nazi supporters in World War II. This was as provocative a document as you could have signed, wasn't it, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, you mentioned paragraph 3 here, and then you simply said that the cadres, the officials from the province should be made accountable, and that's not true. We asked for that -- those steps to be taken not only with respect to the provincial officials but also the republican ones, because of what was going on. They were working against the Serbia in order to create the greater Albanian, and the republican leadership did nothing to prevent that. That was the point we were protesting. We were criticising the republican leadership more than the provincial one. However, we didn't fail to criticise the provincial leadership as well. That's why it was in the first place. The second point was to protest what was going on in Kosovo, the torching, the terror, and so on, and how that was covered up with political speeches, how that would be prevented, how they would put an end to it and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I'm going to have to --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and punish them. However, nobody was ever punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Kosovo Polje meeting just briefly. We've heard evidence about it already. First of all, perhaps you would be good enough to confirm that between the Monday meeting and the Friday meeting while you were getting the people ready to come and speak, a representative of the accused, Mica Jakovljevic, flew down and advised you how to stage manage the event. In particular, advising you to have every word recorded because the press or the various media communication would take it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. That's a false statement. I don't even know who Mica Jakovljevic is. You should verify. Perhaps this person has just heard about me but he doesn't know me, if this refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's your answer, fine. Azem Vllasi, a lawyer, then a political leader, he's a man of peace, isn't he? He's not a man who has ever been engaged in or had suggestions made against him that he's engaged in violence, has he?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Azem Vllasi, all of those who were in the leadership did not personally participate in the violence. However, they protected those who did. Why were people against Azem Vllasi? They were against him because in certain of his public statements, he irritated the citizens. For example, when the journalist Milic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He found himself against you, Solevic, and various other physically very large men at that meeting in Kosovo Polje, and you large men went on to lead demonstrations that bullied and terrorised political leaders into surrender, and you did it on behalf of this accused; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I personally do not know Azem Vllasi. I never saw him in person. You can go and check with him whether we had ever met or greeted each other or exchanged a single word. Never. So you have false information. Somebody deceived you. And as for the rest, the rallies that you are referring to, they were scheduled by the people from the municipalities. In Central Serbia, they didn't know what was actually going on, what things were done against the Serbian people there. Therefore, in municipalities, various local people wanted people to come and state that publicly, and this is why these rallies were organised. There was no organisation standing behind this. There were no nationalist organisations. It was the people. The people asked for that. And as for the petition and me signing the petition, you claimed here that I was the first one to sign it, and I wasn't. I was the first one to criticise the authorities. I always criticised the authorities, and I do that nowadays. And I can tell you that as long as I have lived, I have yet to see good people in power, that would do good for their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of your --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This petition is unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Miroslav Solevic is a very good friend of yours. You and he are in a relation of Kum one to the other, I can't remember which way around it is, and he has been seen saying --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Both of these things are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- with the makers of the film Death of Yugoslavia but the stones were taken, the paving stones were taken, preparatory for use against the police at Kosovo Polje. He's right about that, isn't he? Stones were taken in order to make it a violent event.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. Mr. Nice, you don't know Miroslav Solevic. It would be good if you met him. Let me tell you straight away: There were no stones there. It would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a ludicrous claim, just as to claim that you brought any stones there. What they were doing was expanding the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The AV booth we would need the sound on this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "He brought his executive secretary. He had the executive secretaries. The principal Serbs told them what to say."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you need to interrupt now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to interrupt because I'm pointing to you a completely wrong translation. It says here that Milosevic called his private secretary to relate this to Vllasi, and Vllasi says that the executive secretary of the Central Committee came. This is a huge difference whether this is the executive secretary of the Central Committee, and there were several of them there, and their duty was to travel regularly throughout the country. Milosevic had no private secretary to send there. Once again, this is wrong translation in this BBC footage. You can hear it for yourself. Vllasi, in Albanian, says "sekretari eksekutiv," which is "executive secretary" in Albanian, whereas it's translated as "private secretary." You constantly have wrong translations here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll keep that in mind, Mr. Milosevic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were there just in case. He also says in an interview, the same interview in another part, that they had young men there with pistols, 2 or 300 young men there prepared to do anything. He's right about that, isn't he? This was a planned, violent --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were a party to it.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to move on. If we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me just get what the witness is saying in response to your proposition. In relation to the lorry full of stones, I believe you said earlier in response to Mr. Nice that they were there for the roads. Would you like to elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, gentlemen of the Trial Chamber, the nature of this person that we just saw, Miroslav Solevic, is such that he always gave provocative and -- statements full of jokes to the journalists, and that's his personal choice. You can ask him why he did that. This has nothing to do with reality. If you find another -- another person in Kosovo Polje who can confirm this, I would be ready to allow you to let me hang by the feet and let me hang here for seven hours until my soul departs. I told you the truth. The road was expanded there, and the area around was not cleared. When the police -- I didn't see this, Mr. Robinson. I was inside, and this was happening outside. Police started beating people because there were around 20.000 people around the culture hall. People started fleeing from the police until they reached this construction material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that the comment that we saw attributed to Miroslav Solevic, that was a comment that he made in a jocular manner? He was joking.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purely provocative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what do you say to the other proposition by Mr. Nice that there were other people there with pistols, about 200 people, young men, and they were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police was of mixed composition there. Had there been just a single person with a pistol he would have been disarmed and beaten up. Just a single person with a pistol. So I don't know where he came up with this story. I don't know how he came up with something like this. This is completely untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you may be quite sure in this case --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that is followed by the entire Serbia and Montenegro and rest assured they know that this is not true. They know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you may rest assured that Mr. Solevic has been asked whether he stands by the contents of his interviews and I would not be asking you these questions in this particular case were that not -- were he not to have acknowledged that he does indeed stand by them. I would like you to look at another document from Solevic for your comments. It's a newspaper article that came out on the 10th of February, of 1993 and I want your comment on just a couple passages in it. I think the Chamber has looked at it before. I'm only putting it as an easy way of putting the propositions. In this case I probably won't ask for it to be exhibited but nevertheless it's a useful way of approaching matters. This is an interview by Slavko Curuvija, or, to be precise, the late Slavko Curuvija and Milka Kovacic. And again so the Judges can have a better feel for your community, can you just explain what happened to Slavko Curuvija shortly after the start of the NATO bombing. He was a journalist. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I lived in Kosovo Polje, or rather, in Pristina. I have lived there for the last ten years and what I know about that comes from the newspapers. I couldn't give you anything more than that, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by the secret police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something for you to say. I can't say anything about that, nothing at all, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can't say something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at the bottom of the first page, please. In the --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You should have got the -- at the bottom you should have got the -- if the usher would be good enough to take the --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in hospital at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is what your very good friend Solevic said about Novi Sad. You can see on the bottom left-hand corner in your version the question, "It's well known what happened in Novi Sad," and Solevic replied this: "Other things are well known too. The rallies started and brought down the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have -- we haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In your version it's the first page in the English. It's the third document, I'm told. It's got the words "Feature 11" in the top right-hand corner, and it's dated the 10th of February, 1993. Sorry not to have dealt with that more carefully. And it's towards the bottom of the page where Solevic said this: "Other things are known, too. The rallies started and brought down the leaderships of Vojvodina and Montenegro." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The rallies started and brought down the leaderships of Vojvodina and Montenegro. We had prepared everything to overthrow the Bosnian leadership too. We thought that the thing would be carried out the easiest over there. But Sloba and Serbian leadership asked us to give up Jajce. It was a mistake that he stopped us. He could, as he had done up to that point, played dumb at their pressure, until we wipe off Bosnia." Now, Mr. Bulatovic, again I'm looking at the integration of all these matters together; your Serb nationalist activities and changes in Montenegro, Vojvodina, and in Bosnia. Will you confirm, please, that there was indeed a planned rally at Jajce in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing about such a rally, and we are best men, we are Kums. It is true, though, that he lives nowadays in Nis and I live elsewhere, but this is the first time that I hear about this rally in Jajce. As I've told you, he had a tendency to joke when giving statements, and it would be best if the Tribunal were to call him here to clarify this. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Tribunal to decide. You have no reason to doubt what he says about a planned demonstration in Jajce, do you? And I must suggest to you a little more why it didn't happen. See if this jogs your memory. Drasko Milicevic, coordinator for the Central Committee, communicated between you and the Central Committee and thus this accused, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and the planned demonstration at Jajce --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any Drasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- was cancelled because at that time the accused communicated to you demonstrators that he wanted the Bosnian votes and that he wouldn't get the Bosnian votes if -- that he needed in the Presidency or in the committee, I'm not sure which, but he wouldn't get the Bosnian votes if that demonstration went ahead, and that's why it was cancelled and that's why Solevic said it was cancelled. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're asking me about things that I know nothing about. I don't know anything about that portion. You're not asking me about what I testified about here. You're not trying to verify whether I said something that wasn't true. As for these other things, I can't testify about that. You should ask Solevic why he gave these interviews and why he mentioned this rally in Jajce. As far as I know, that rally was never organised, nor was its organisation ever discussed. He called me Colonel. That was the name that he used for me. And after that, the people started using that in a jocular way, in a fun way. That's his nature. He likes to joke with people. But there was no ill intention there. He never hurt anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Chamber would go on to the second -- the next page, rather, and the witness would stay with the passage of the text a little further on. He says as to the rift of the rally staff that Solevic said he wanted to dissolve the rally staff, that no decision could be taken without Kosta, Bosko, Dusko Ristic and himself. Milosevic said no, i.e., that the rally staff should not be disbanded but then a month later said that it should be. Does that fit with your recollection of history, that eventually it was the accused himself who insisted that the rally staff be disbanded? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was neither any staff -- I know nothing about that. This is the first time I hear of that staff. You keep using the words nationalists and group of nationalists, Mr. Nice. Such group never existed. Had it existed I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple more questions because I don't have any more time although I have a lot more I would like to ask you. To take Vojvodina as an example, the way your demonstrations worked is this: Mob rule on streets, political pressure from Belgrade, came together to frighten the leaders into giving up. That's what you did, wasn't it? I'm not quoting from the article, I'm putting a proposition to you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This term you're using, "mob," to refer to the people, to people looking for salvation, I think is offensive. However, this is not your term, it wasn't coined by you, it was coined by the political leadership of Kosovo. The defenseless people they referred to as mob, these defenseless people who only asked to have equal status. I would kindly ask you not to refer to them as a mob. It was not a mob. These were just misfortunate people. Let me tell you what happened on the 17th of March, 2004. Do you think that that was the mob or the people asking to be helped? The KFOR was there, the representatives of the UN were there, and all the while they were going on with killing people and destroying their homes, and you think that they're all mob?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To take an example of Vojvodina, a province with a long history of autonomy, dating back to the Austro-Hungarian times, seen throughout Yugoslavia as a model of interethnic co-existence and a place where the Serbs were, by the relevant time, about two-thirds majority, was a place that you invaded on 13 different demonstrations, you and your group, I don't mean you necessarily on every one, on the last time settling in for two full days. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I attended the first rally, which was not really a rally, but what happened was that 2.000 groups -- 2.000 Serbs went to the Assembly of Serbia in order to inform them about the position of the Serbian people in Kosovo and Metohija and to ask Vojvodina as a province, which supported the authorities because of its own interests, without knowing what the authorities in Kosovo and Metohija were in fact supporting and how they were ignoring the terror against the Serbian people in Kosovo and Metohija. They didn't let us enter the Assembly building. They didn't give us any water or provide any power to us. Nobody went there to bring down the authorities. They did that themselves through their positions and views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you when I first asked you questions what on earth --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krunic and the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what on earth right Kosovo Serbs had to be bringing down political leaders in Montenegro and in Vojvodina and I must suggest to you the answer is that this was not just limited to Kosovo Serbs --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo Serbs did not do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Kosovo Serbs did not do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Find the footage -- find the footage showing that where their authorities toppled the authorities and see if there was a single person from Kosovo present there. There was nobody there, Mr. Nice, and you can bring out any kind of ridiculous accusations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man you say in your own interview "soared to the throne on the shoulder of the Serbian resistance movement" was never a leader with an ideological platform but he was a man whose taste for power you stimulated by letting him espouse your cause. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody joined us. Your claims are tendentious. Nobody joined us in achieving our interests. We asked him to come, and later on we asked Dr. Zoran Grujic to come to Kosovo Polje. And now that you have mentioned, I have to mention him, too, Mr. Azem Vllasi, Kole Shiroka, Agim Heripi [phoen], that entire group which sat with him in the culture hall in Kosovo Polje, listening to what these unfortunate people were saying. Over 70 speakers informed them about everything that was done against the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija. However, you do not care about that. All you care are the quotations showing this or that. Well, we were not lawyers, we could not write this document any better than we did. We did it in the best way we could. However, we addressed certain people that we expected would help us. Now, let me tell you this: The Albanians in Kosovo, if certain of their rights were violated, why didn't they write a petition to them and have this issue raised of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what rights of theirs were violated? They did not have a single reason to complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have time to go into everything, but don't you remember after 1981, the students' demonstration, the one that may have been generated by the KGB or by some other intelligence agency, the students indeed did petition against the oppressive response of the authorities. Don't you remember that? Don't you remember the 1981 students' petition complaining at the wrong treatment of the students?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are fewer manipulations. What KGB are you talking about? The CIA had its fingers there and it's all coming to surface now. At the time we didn't know that. Now we're knowing where worm had come from. The rotten apple was placed in a bushel of good apples and it turned the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entire bushel rotten and we are just learning about this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you spoke in your interview of letting the genie out of the bottle, that was a phrase that gave way to the truth, wasn't it? By your actions you let this accused out and into positions of power by which he did enormous damage to the former Yugoslavia, and you know that it's in part your responsibility for having given him power.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you are bringing up this minor provocation which was used in order to prompt the leadership to take even minor steps in Kosovo and now you're saying that this is why Yugoslavia fell apart? No. If you had not interfered, Yugoslavia would still be existing now. Sir, Yugoslavia was destroyed by those who created it, those who signed the Versailles treaty, and later on those who were figures in the Second World War. Those are the people who destroyed Yugoslavia. Tito in Jajce divided Yugoslavia based on national principles, and he created these two provinces within Serbia. Dalmatia, Lika, and Krajina and Banija were not created as provinces, were not established as provinces. Mr. Nice, this is tendentiously aimed against Serbian nation and Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baranja was taken away from Serbia and Vojvodina and given to Croatia and it had never been part of Croatia before. Do you think that that was the right decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question, totally different, matter of credit only, it's to do with your conduct in this courtroom. I just simply remind you that throughout your answers you've referred to the accused as "Mr. President," you've used either the term "Mr." for the Judges - once you referred to His Honour Judge Robinson as Judge Robinson - and you've referred to them as the "gentlemen of the Court." When you first came here, and you can obviously read, you didn't read the words on the card of the solemn declaration and you gave your own format of wording. Was that intentional?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I give an oath -- are you referring to the oath? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering why you didn't --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I give an oath, gentlemen, I -- in the end I read that text, but prior to that I swore to my faith. I swore on my dignity and on my honour that I would say the truth, and following that I read out the text that the usher gave me, the Tribunal's text. So my intentions were the most honourable ones, and I fully -- I expressed my full respect to this Tribunal, both to Mr. Robinson and to Mr. Kwon and to Mr. Bonomy. I expressed my deepest --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- respect, and I don't think that I hurt or offended this Tribunal in any way, nor you, for that matter, regardless of the fact that you put some provocative and tendentious questions to me. But that doesn't matter. You're a Prosecutor. Perhaps you're entitled to that and I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this Court, do you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are near the time. We are beyond the time for the break. What is the question you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does he accept the legality of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't think we need to go into that, Mr. Nice, at this stage. We'll take the break now for 20 minutes. And when we come back, we'll deal with the documents which you wish to have exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibits. The '94 petition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the first document we looked at today, to which reference is made in the 1994 newspaper article, which was the second document we looked at today and which, as His Honour Judge Kwon observed, has the witness acknowledging that he was the first signatory of the petition. I'd ask for those to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not minded to tender the petition of January 1986?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. That was on the last occasion. Yes, that should be the first exhibit, the petition of 1986, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 859.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for being reminded about that. Then the petition of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I deal with the objections in relation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The document referred to by Mr. Nice referring to the 1994 petition, I think there may be some confusion relating to this document. The answer when the witness was first presented with the document was that he was not the first signatory and his answer was that he couldn't remember signing the document. Your Honour Judge Kwon referred to the interview with Mr. Bulatovic where there was reference to Mr. Bulatovic being the first signatory to the letter or, rather, the new petition, and the answer in relation to that, it was my recollection, was that this witness spoke to the 1986 petition but did not speak to and had nothing to do with the 1994 petition. I stand to be corrected if that's not right, but that was my recollection, Your Honour, concerning that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think his answer overall might have started off by saying he didn't remember signing that petition or being the first person to sign it but eventually he wasn't challenging the possibility that he had done. After all, his answers in the newspaper interview, which he did not say were fictional or untrue, are quite clear that he was acknowledging signing that document. It's unfortunate that the only copy we've been able to obtain doesn't have the first signature but starts at number 6, but in my submission there is plenty of connecting material for there this petition to go in. And in any event, it is a document of significance in the chronology of events because the existence of that petition as part of the pressure that the witness acknowledged he was applying to the Serb leadership is an important part of the chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the document as a whole and the evidence as a whole in terms of the witness's testimony, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the interview with the witness on the 21st of October of 1994 in Nin newspaper or magazine, may that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document to which I turned was the English translation of the document put in by the accused a couple of weeks ago, which was the 1985 petition. I'm neutral as to whether the translation which we provided goes in as part of his exhibit, which was entirely untranslated, or if it should go in separately as our exhibit. It may be that in case there is ever a question on some aspect of the translation it's better it goes in as our exhibit, although it's duplication of the petition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excerpts from Sleepless Nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Dicklich says that in fact the petition, although looked at and referred to by the witness in the course of his evidence being led wasn't produced, so that therefore the 1985 petition should go in as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, I think, was the -- the next physical document was the interview record with Miroslav Solevic, as I explained to you, that's been looked at before and not admitted. I'm -- obviously I would prefer it to be an exhibit because it's a contemporaneous or more contemporaneous record of interviews but I'm in the Court's hands on that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. -- We will not admit this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The video of Solevic talking about the stones we've looked at before, and again I'm not going to press that in light of the Court's earlier approach to that. The witness had an opportunity of seeing it and commented on it, and he didn't deny that the things were said, he gave an explanation for their being said but that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will not admit this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a very short extract of a BBC programme. The witness objected to its being selected. You'll remember it is the short passage where he expresses his emotions at the death of somebody on a battlefield 600 and more years ago. In fact I only played that short extract for want of time. We have, if the accused or the witness wants to see it, what we believe to be all the parts of that programme that have him speaking. That apart, but I simply make that clear that's available if anybody wants to see it, but my request is that the passage that was played should be exhibited, that single clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- just only that part. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the assigned counsel we do query the relevance of that and we note that it was only a small extract, which is of concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We hear you, Ms. Higgins, but we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to admit that excerpt from Mr. Bulatovic's interview, the BBC clip, I mean, I think it would only be fair to play it for Mr. Bulatovic so he can hear what he says. He could not hear what he said, and you cannot really rely on the English translation in the subtitles, and it was incorrect many times. So this was not the usual procedure that was applied. Actually, the witness did not see the exhibit in a language that he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
