utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say that if the BBC played only that -- I don't know what they played, but if they played only that, that is purely tendentious because I took them to -- so that they could see a Serb village, and there is nothing left of that Serb village there. Not a single stone was left there. The cemetery was razed. The houses were razed. And they cut out all of that, apparently, and they only showed what I said by the monument where the two rulers had been killed, and it's only natural that any people will defend their own state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have it played in re-examination if you wish. Your re-examination, is there any?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please commence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I thought that you wished to finish something else before I started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to clarify one thing, Mr. Bulatovic. What Mr. Nice said to you when you say -- he said that when you say "Siptar" that you offend Albanians. Did you ever hear anyone insulting Albanians when they called them Siptars?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any such thing in all my life, and I can take an oath on -- as far as that is concerned. I can swear with my son's life. God gave me a son only when I was 59, and I can swear on that only son's life that I never heard of that as being offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the public gallery they have different channels in terms of how they can listen to different languages? So the channel number 3 is called "Shqip." That is the Albanian language on that list of languages.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that somebody from this administration wrote that list of languages out. If you are insulting them when you say "Siptars," that should mean that they also offend Albanians when they say "Sip." Do you find that logical, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that quite logical. I tell you I was totally perplexed when I heard that question today. I know a whole army of Albanian people in Kosovo and no one was ever offended when I said to them that they were Siptars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We are going to deal with this petition very briefly now, the petition from the book called Sleepless Nights, and that is the petition that you had signed. That is the petition from 1985.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice quoted the second paragraph of that petition to you. It wasn't very accurately translated, but I'm going to quote it yet again, this second paragraph in the Serbian language, because the point was in the use of the words "genocide" and "fascist." The second paragraph reads as follows of this petition that you signed: "The situation in reality is a terrible one. A part of Yugoslavia was occupied, part of our national being, and genocide against us Serbs by Albanian fascism in Kosovo has received the right to -- to exist."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the sentence, and I'll go on. Before I put a question to you now in relation to what Mr. Nice said, he said that you were a nationalist because you mentioned genocide, I'm going to read out a quotation to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have already quoted that text. That is the text of Ivan Kristan, a Slovenian professor who testified here, and this text comes from his article published in the periodical called Socialism in 1981, that is to say four years before this petition was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that article, Mr. Kristan says -- Please listen to this, Mr. Bulatovic, very carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. The interpreters do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters do not have the text and they're asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. I'm going to read it very slowly and it's a very brief quotation anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "The irredentist aspirations of the Albanian nationalists in Kosovo are not a recent development. Actually, they appear as the extension of various quisling and fascist organisations that fought during the war against the National Liberation Movement of the Yugoslav peoples," and so on and so forth. So this would be my question, Mr. Bulatovic: Before you even wrote this petition, was it not generally known that events in Kosovo and Metohija were aimed at chauvinism, Albanian separatism, and the expulsion of Serbs, that they were an extension of this Balist fascist movement during the Second World War, they convey back to the times of Hitler and Mussolini?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... leading or tendentiously extended question and I'm not sure that any answer to it is going to assist the Chamber very much. It's really the accused's argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question is leading. You'll have to reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bulatovic, you who wrote this petition, were you the first to mention Balists and fascists carrying out genocide in Kosovo and Metohija or was this mentioned very extensively?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A countless number of times in different newspapers this was mentioned, and I know about it too. The first day when I testified here, Mr. Robinson, I pointed out that during the war, rather towards the end of the Second World War, Fadil Hoxha transferred all of them -- sorry, not all of them. They called themselves Balists. They were fascists. He managed to get some of them to join the partisan movements, and then they came to join the partisan communist movements in Drenica. That is how they operated and that is how Zenel Hajdini detachment was established and Fadil Hoxha was its commander. This detachment had only three Serbs; Darlic [phoen], Lakicovic [phoen] and Mihailo Radulovic Kacak. All three of them had Albanian names. Had they known who these three men were, they would have killed all of them. That is why Vuko Popovic, a commander of a partisan detachment in Drenica was killed. When they realised that the commander was a Serb at the first meeting of their staff, they killed him. So they simply changed sides and they came to join the Communist Party after having been fascists. They functioned after the Second World War as they did, but people are the way they are, and they could not have assumed all of these things. And it was only in the 1970s that we realised where this worm came from, as it were, and no one would -- no one would ever have thought of them joining the ranks of terrorists. No one could realise that that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice quoted a few paragraphs of this petition to you, though incompletely. So I will go through these paragraphs in order to see whether this is some kind of a Serbian nationalist claim. Paragraph 1 reads as follows: "They should put on the agenda certain claims." Obviously you are addressing the two parliaments. You want the parliaments to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the objective of the petition. We expected them to have extraordinary sessions, special sessions of the Assembly devoted to that and that they would discuss the matters raised in the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in this petition you ask for the parliaments to place these questions on their agendas.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first demand, number one, says here: "To carry out our basic human rights on the basis of the SFRY constitution and international conventions and which have absolutely been denied us." Is that the first demand that you had?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first demand in its entirety. We did not ask for any more rights than other people but we did not agree to lesser rights either and we did not want anybody to terrorise us or persecute us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Nice says that you asked for removals, et cetera, et cetera, and that is paragraph 3: "To immediately remove from the authorities of the province and the republic and to hold accountable Greater Albanian chauvinists who are in charge of the rebellion in Kosovo and who want to make it possible for Greater Albanian chauvinists to take over Yugoslavia. We ask for them to be held responsible, and also cadres of Serb ethnicity who are serving this ideology." So is that the point, to make it impossible for Greater Albanian separatists to function, regardless of whether this has to do with commission or non-commission on the part of Albanians or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should be held responsible before the authorities, and all of those who tacitly supported all of this against the Serbian people. Like Fadil Hoxha. He was the main person in charge of this ideology that was carried through in Kosovo and Metohija. Perhaps it's shameful that I'm talking about a dead man this way, so it wouldn't be right to speak of a dead person in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice said that you advocated the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija. Paragraph 5 reads as follows. I'm going to read it: "That no hospitality should be offered to emigres from Albania who settled as of the 6th of April 1941 to the present day, regardless of whether they came to settle under Mussolini's programme or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. later on according to Enver Hoxha's programme." Mr. Bulatovic, are you asking that the Albanians be expelled from Kosovo or are you asking that hospitality be withheld to immigrants from Albanian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before that question is answered, what was said in relation to the expulsion of Kosovo Albanians was not spoken of in respect of the period 1985 but of course in respect of much later. I observe, I don't object to the questions being asked, but simply for the sake of the Court's record, that lack of time meant I certainly didn't address every issue in this petition which was first raised in the course of examination-in-chief and dealt with very briefly, and I certainly didn't deal one way or another with the propositions advanced by Enver Hoxha and it certainly shouldn't be interpreted as our accepting what is said here about Enver Hoxha. I make no points beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. Answer the question, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we demanded was this: That from -- that the Albanian emigrants be sent back from Kosovo and Metohija who came in to settle there, and the main violence came from them. The Albanians who were autochthonous and lived there for three centuries and were born there, they wanted to stir them up and work for their Albanian separatist positions. So we know where the harm was coming from. We knew where the rotten apple had come from and we wanted to get rid of the rotten apple so that the people who had lived there forever could continue to live in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, the point of the quotation I read out, would it be this: To deny hospitality to those who came in pursuant to Mussolini and Enver Hoxha's programmes; is that right? Nobody else, it didn't refer to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody else, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since Mr. Nice brought this up a moment ago and said that you later on demanded the colonisation, although that word was never used, I'm going to quote point 7, what you in fact demanded. That is all listed in point 7: "We demand that under the supervision of the republican and federal authorities without fail we see the return of expelled Serb families," that that be enabled.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So does this refer to the return of the Serb families who were expelled from Kosovo during the terror waged by the Albanian separatists, regardless of whether it took place during Mussolini after World War II but it referred to people who were expelled from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Robinson and Your Honours the Judges in the Trial Chamber, what we demanded was that all expulsed Serbs be allowed to return, all the Serbs who had to leave the area as a result of Albanian and Balist terrorists, and after World War II there was terror and the terrorists expelled them. They were working under cover and worked individually to begin with. So we did not demand any people who were living there as peacefully, autochthonous people who were born there, we had no problems with those people. But others were given support by the fascists, the Balists, they gained support, and that was where the problem came from and that's what ultimately led to the war as well. Had the petition been placed on the agenda perhaps a lot of what subsequently happened might have been avoided and everybody would have been satisfied but nobody batted an eye to this petition. We could have written a hundred petitions, whereas nobody prevented Albanians, if they had been damaged in any way or disadvantaged, to write their own petition and address it to the same leadership and then we would see whether they would have taken any steps if they had done that, but they didn't do that. They sought assistance from forces outside the country. We, on the other hand, were aboveboard and asked assistance for the powers that be in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your petition do you see anything there -- can you quote any passage there, any of your demands which would be discriminatory towards the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. There's none of that there. There's nothing like that there. They attacked me and criticised me for the speech I held in Studenica on the 18th of May 1986, for example, to mark the celebrations of 800 years of Studenica itself, and Mr. Azem Vllasi, the then-president of the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Kosovo at the time asked the state security service to send them the contents of the speech that was delivered by Kosta Bulatovic in Studenica. He thought that I might have said something against the Albanian people. And when he received the text of my speech, and I have it in my attache case if you want me to read it out before the Trial Chamber for the purpose of truth so that we can complete all this -- complete this discussion, when he read the text of the speech he just stood there and said, well, I really have nothing to say, because he was told by his associates something else and he said I have no criticisms to make of the speech. That's what Azem himself said, and you can ask him whether he had any criticisms of my speech delivered at the Studenica monastery at the celebrations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice said, and I made a note of that, in asking you a question or making a comment of his own, I don't remember that detail now, anyway he said that in 1995 I started attacking the Kosovo Albanians in response to your petition and the demands you laid down. And similarly, he said that there were individual violence, that there was no organised violence. Now, do you know anything about the organising of an illegal Albanian SUP in Kosovo and Metohija? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't meddle with intelligence services. I don't associate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about intelligence services, I'm talking about public information.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, publicly speaking, we saw that there were things that were happening that had been organised. We even saw footage from Cicavica and a teacher there and what happened to him, but I think that the whole of Europe saw that footage when this person made a statement, he was armed and wearing a uniform, and we couldn't believe that that had happened. We thought that it was individuals who were doing things like that, just as Mr. Nice has been saying. But after that television footage, we became aware that there was a dangerous organisation afoot and that radical measures were unavoidable and that ultimately this would lead to war in Kosovo and Metohija because it was their aim to bring about a war with the help of people from outside, and that is what came to pass. Now, I'm a man of the people. I'm not a politician. But I was part of the politics that went on there and of course we weren't satisfied with the solutions and with the situation. We thought that if we went to our leadership, they would take steps to better our lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We want shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, gentlemen, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that during the testimony of Judge Danica Marinkovic, an exhibit contained in tab 4 during her testimony contained an indictment against members of the illegal SUP in Kosovo and Metohija, and among other things, I have it here once again, the number is KT, that is the Prosecution number, 101/94 is the number of that document I'm referring to. It is a criminal report dated 1994 in the Prosecution, and it could not have been the product of something that took place, as Mr. Nice said, in 1995 because it was a 1994 document. So if something precedes a date cannot be the result and consequence of something that happened if it happened before the event itself. And this has been tendered into evidence and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I ask you, Mr. Bulatovic, that since this is a public trial, do you happen to remember that a large number of members belonging to the illegal SUP were uncovered and they were working to create armed formations in order to cut Kosovo and Metohija off from the rest of the country?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was public. Nothing was clandestine there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was clandestine. All the trials were public and open.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the document in English, it has been translated, and you'll be able to find it, gentlemen, in tab 4. It is within Judge Danica Marinkovic's testimony and the documents produced there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nice said that I met your demands. Now, I'm asking you this: Since he said that I met your demands and that the consequence of that was that many Albanians were killed and expelled -- that's what Mr. Nice said, words to that effect. Now, tell me this: Were your demands to kill any Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it. I said in my statement, and I address myself to Mr. Robinson, I said that we did not ask anything, any reprisals against anybody because evil begets evil and we would have been doing evil to ourselves. So we never opted for that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic, so your demands were not that Albanians should be killed. Now, were your demands that the Albanians should be expelled?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have that demand either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't want them to be expelled or killed, did you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down, thank you, and make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you hear that from the interpreters? And Mr. Bulatovic. You have to observe a pause between question and answer in the interests of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice said that there was no organised violence. Now we can see that the illegal MUP was organised and had been organised. Now, what else was organised? Did they organise dismissal or removal from people leaving their jobs to form separatist movements?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- that did happen en masse and we were astonished to see this process taking place. We wondered who was supporting it and how this came about and what was happening in our country. Without any reason at all, people were leaving schools, they were leaving their jobs. At the various institutions very few people remained. People were leaving the municipality. There was nobody to replace them in their work posts. Quite simply, we were taken aback. What was all that about? What was happening? And that was the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since throughout that time you lived in Kosovo yourself, you were there, were you able to notice any measures of discrimination towards Albanians on the part of the Serb authorities or from the Serbs themselves?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President and Mr. Robinson, the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija enjoyed beneficial rights and positions everywhere. I remember when I was a young man Rade Jekenovic [phoen], for example, somebody from my village, was president of the party and he assigned -- he gave me an assignment. There was an officer from Belgrade, his name was Popovic, and he brought a football and told us to go to an Albanian village and play football together with their children so that they would socialise with us and be friends with us and we wanted to demonstrate this by playing football with them. It was difficult to get them to go to school at all and study, and that's the truth of it. Now it turns out that we exercised terror over them. It was quite two reverse opinions, two opposite opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice asked you why you reacted emotionally to the death of the Turkish Tzar Murat. Now, I didn't understand the question fully but he did show you some sort of footage. So might we have that same footage shown that we can all see your reactions to the death of the Turkish Tzar whose name was Murat and who died almost 620 years ago.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two rulers died on that occasion. The Serb Tzar or, rather, Prince Lazar, and the Turkish Tzar Murat. They were both killed. And I've never seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are quoting folklore there. It is an epic poem that you are in fact quoting.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by Radovan Becirevic, who wrote the famous epic poem The Battle of Kosovo Polje. So I quoted from his epic poem to celebrate this event, and shame be on the journalist from Great Britain for having presented this in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was the journalist made aware that you were quoting from this epic poem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just said it was a poet who wrote that epic poem, and I was quoting the verses. In the Serbian language, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian we can see that it is a poem because we have rhymes there, whereas the journalist was -- well, yes. You were reciting the epic poem. He was taken to the spot where this took place and then you were in fact reciting the poem, were you not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. We have dealt with that exhibit. You can introduce it into evidence as much as you like, but this just shows the nature of the exhibits that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They're quite unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they're unimportant. I think they're important because they were used tendentiously.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, you're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that the whole object ought to be seen by the accused or others in order to be seen whether this is used tendentiously or simply to reflect what this witness in that programme was seeking to do. My position, as always, is that I'm so pressed for time I simply can't take extended periods of time with material like this. It's available if they want to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm beginning to be disturbed by the constant references to the pressure of time. We have been at pains, and obviously are not succeeding in satisfying everyone, but at pains to try to give both parties equivalent time to present their cases, and that is because everyone understands the difficulty of dealing with a trial of this magnitude within a reasonable time, and it's for the parties to select what they present. Now, if you present a snippet of a film and then discover that there's an answer to the point, then that's the end of it, surely. And it is very disturbing then to hear a complaint that that's done simply for lack of time. It's a matter of preparation and presentation of what will be helpful to us, hopefully, within the time that has been fairly allotted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a complaint, simply a recognition of the pressures that are on us. In an example like this, it's not a question of saying, so far as I'm concerned, that there's an answer to the point we made. I'm simply making the point in answer to the accused's assertion that something has been taken out of context, that it's all available if he wishes to see it. I have always to decide how many of the issues that are available can be explored in part or fully, and those are the difficulties under which I labour. But it's certainly not a complaint, Your Honour, I'm just simply identifying the realities. If I may say so, taking for example this witness, there are many issues I haven't been able to explore with them that I would like to have done. I've only identified one, which was the Enver Hoxha point, for fear of there being an inference that by not dealing with it I waived any objections to the point raised by the witness, and I didn't seek to do any more than that. Again, this is not in any sense a complaint, it's simply identifying from time to time the problems and the possible solutions to them. But Your Honour, that's all I have to say on it. As to this particular clip, which is indeed very short, I don't press any solution, I simply make the point that it is available if anybody wanted to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. I don't think the case will stand or fall on the basis of this clip and I certainly don't wish to hear any more of it. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice claimed that I had sent some sort of executive secretary from the Central Committee to tell you what you ought to say at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mica Jakovljevic was the name.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Regardless of whether you know him or not it's not important at all. Under the circumstances in which you lived, in the protests that you expressed, was there anyone there who could have come from Belgrade -- was it possible for anyone to come from Belgrade and tell you what you ought to say?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had we heard that, we wouldn't have been in the situation that we were in. We were simply lost people. We were wondering what to do. We were sending petitions. Nobody paid attention to them. Protest rallies were held wherever violence had been committed. For example, in Prekale we held a protest rally and in that protest rally people spoke out. I wasn't there in the village but that is the only village in the world where under the pressure of Albanian fascists and nationalists they put a board in the village where they wrote out names. Out of 22 Serb houses, all were put on sale. The entire village was put on sale. I don't think that there's another case like that in the world. There was, for example, another photograph with a woman bearing a weapon with two children following her having pitchforks and then two girls carrying buckets for water. So this gives you an impression of what kind of people lived there. This is simply something that defies explanation. I would need at least two years to tell you about all of the events, and we would need people to go to the site, to the locations there and talk to the people who lived there in order to uncover the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice said something about the rally in Kosovo Polje and the time when the incident broke out between the police and the citizens and said that this had been planned, the violence had been planned. Do you know anything about that? Do you know about anyone planning any violence?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guarantee you here before this Chamber, you can put me on trial if anybody can substantiate and prove this. As for the jokes, that's another matter. But seriously looking, that was impossible. I lived in Kosovo Polje. How could something happen there without me knowing about that, without other people knowing about that? This was a joke, a pure joke and nothing more than a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Nice said that 200 people had pistols, that they were armed. First of all, tell us, did anybody fire during that rally?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody see or hear anybody having a pistol?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is completely untrue. You have to realise something: Had there been a single person with a weapon there, and police followed and monitored everything closely, God knows what would have happened to that person who was armed. There was undoubtedly no weapons there. I told those people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness can't really say whether anybody saw or heard anybody having a pistol, but continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it beyond dispute that there was no use of weapons there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely beyond dispute. This is a pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, do you remember that in the papers a report of the commission of the federal SUP was published about how the police used force against citizens without justification. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Nice asked you what right the Kosovo Serbs had to topple the government in Vojvodina and Montenegro. When I -- did you - and when I say you I don't mean just you personally, I mean other Kosovo Serbs as well - did you ever go to topple the government in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. You didn't. Did you go to Montenegro and Vojvodina seeking help?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief when we discussed your activities, did we have any questions regarding your visits to the leadership of Montenegro where you sought help?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we gave brief replies then to those questions. I can repeat it again before the Trial Chamber. There were eight of us who went to the Central Committee of Montenegro. We were supposed to meet with Dobroslav Culafic, who was the president of the Central Committee of Montenegro. Instead of him, the then-secretary of the Central Committee, Vuksanovic, met with us, as did member of the Central Committee Angl Kokovacovic [phoen]. The meeting lasted some two hours. We informed them about everything that was being done against our people in Kosovo and Metohija, and we asked him, can you help us in any way? Can you help us in order to put an end to this so that we can survive in that area? If you cannot help us, then just tell us. So tell us openly that you would not support this so that we can all collectively move out. This is the truth. This is why on the 20th of June, 1986, there was a mass exodus, and the police stopped the column of people leaving. I went to Belgrade on the first day, and the state security arrested me in the house of Mijo -- Mijo in Baric. And I was already near Belgrade, and the police halted the column of people leaving with their household goods and so on. They didn't want the people leaving at the time, and now it would suit them very well if those people left the territory, which is going to happen in the nearest future. However, they will not blame a group of nationalists for that as they did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bulatovic. So you went to Montenegro in order to inform the authorities of your problems. You had no intention to topple any government.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the end, Mr. Nice told you that the student demonstrations in 1981, allegedly 1981 demonstrations, broke out as a result of repression against Albanians and students. Are you aware of any repression that was carried out and that led the students to rebel, or do you know the actual reasons of the 1981 demonstrations in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is not true that there was any repression there. The reason was that they, in those demonstrations, sought the status of republic for Kosovo. Last time Tito was in Kosovo in the Grand Hotel it seems that he said there will be no Greater Albania. Kosovo and Metohija will not be detached from Serbia. You have to accept this, leave in peace and be loyal citizens in this province and Serbia, and they were dissatisfied. When Tito died, after a year or so they organised these demonstrations, Mr. Robinson. That's what they did. And they publicly sought the status of republic for Kosovo. They never came out with a claim that there was any terror against them, no. Their slogan was "Kosovo Republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I would like just to give a brief statement, with your leave. I would like to address myself to the Trial Chamber before leaving for Montenegro, with your permission. It is going to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, gentlemen of the Trial Chamber, before I go home I would like to tell you something. First of all, in accordance with your decision of last week on Thursday, on the 5th of May I am to return to Hague to answer charges for contempt of court. Second, what I would like to state now is that I came here as a Defence witness in the presentation of evidence of Mr. Milosevic with best intention. Not even -- it did not even occur to me that any problems could arise. Three, in the presence of the president, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, I answered all questions, his questions and the Prosecutor's questions, and I believe that I expressed my respect to all of the parties here. Fourth, in the absence of the president, Mr. Milosevic, therefore, in totally -- under totally new circumstances, I could not continue testifying. Five, my intention was not to obstruct or slow down in any way the proceedings. On the contrary, my intention from the very beginning was and remains to contribute to the establishing of truth and insist in the administration of justice in fair -- in a fair situation. The justice and dignity are the most important principles for me, and after two weeks I'm going home with a completely clear conscience, realising that I have fulfilled my obligation with respect to the truth, to the justice, to my people, to my country and my president. In the end, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to wish all the best to my president Mr. Milosevic, hoping to see him soon in Belgrade. I would like to thank you for your patience for having listened to me, because I'm not a politician and it is probable that I did not always express myself in the best possible way and was perhaps sometimes too long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I deal with an administrative matter related to an earlier witness's exhibits to use this time while this witness is withdrawing. The Chamber will recall Exhibits 856 and 856.1 in the evidence of Dobricanin were documents prepared by my learned friend Mr. Saxon, analysing findings about fingerprints according to contemporaneous documents. Mr. Saxon has diligently gone through the material and found that there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has found that there are two names that he omitted from the first versions of these documents, and with your leave I substitute for 856 and 856.1, new versions of those documents. If we distribute them you will see where the two additional names are. They're on the first page and they're numbers about six and seven on that page. The additional references can be seen on the first page. Two names, about six and seven, and the fact that they've been recorded on the document itself so I hope that the record will not be confusing at any stage. Mustafa Asllani and Hakip Imeri are the two names. I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Before the next witness is called, I'll give the Chamber's decision in relation to Judge Markovic's exhibits -- Marinkovic's evidence. These arose during cross-examination. The Article B92, The Disturbing Truth of 8 March 2002 by Natasa Kandic. This was a news article that was not accepted by the witness, is not admitted. Next, the article in Borba concerning the petition, that was withdrawn. Next, the ten medical certificates describing injuries in the police case. There is no dispute over authenticity. These are to be admitted as one exhibit in ten tabs. I am just waiting for the court deputy to give that a number. That was ten medical certificates describing injuries in the police case. Those are to be admitted as one exhibit in ten tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 864.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. Next, a complaint by Fazli Bala [phoen], the telegram from him to the minister of interior and his complaint to the district court. There is no dispute over authenticity. These are all admitted as one exhibit in three tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will be 865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next, the Spotlight Report number 16. Nothing was established through the witness. This is not admitted. Next, the statement and videos of three Kosovo Albanians introduced to challenge prior statements that were members of the KLA. This is not admitted. The last item is the Official Note by the prosecutor concerning Racak, which is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 866.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't hear that. Microphone for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Mr. Jasovic. I see him walking in as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let the witness make the declaration. Make the declaration. Read what is on the paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, you may commence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, tell us, please, where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of September, 1953, in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of education have you had? What schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: In Pec I completed secondary school and elementary school, and I reached my final examinations at the faculty of security at the University of Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the events in Kosovo took place, those that are being dealt with here, and you were at that time employed by the Ministry of Interior, tell me, since when have you been employed in the Ministry of Interior of Serbia or, rather, do you still work there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac on the 1st of July, 1975. I still work there as a crime investigation policeman or, rather, an inspector at the SUP of Urosevac which has been provisionally relocated to Leskovac since 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly what sectors you worked in in that period from 1975 when you said that you were first employed by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: From 1975 until May 1981, I worked as a policeman at the police station in Stimlje. The Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac is in charge of that police station. In May 1981, I was appointed assistant commander of the police station in Urosevac, and I worked there until 1986. In 1986, I started working in the crime prevention department within the general crime section in Urosevac. I worked there as a crime investigation policeman or, rather, an inspector, and that is the job I -- I have until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your work in Stimlje, for almost 20 years you've been an inspector at the police station in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your previous answers, can it be inferred that you are quite familiar with the municipality of Stimlje both in terms of the population, their mutual relations, geography, the configuration of the terrain in Stimlje? I see that you worked there for many years, and anyway, Stimlje is in the area of SUP Urosevac where you work until the present day. So can it be inferred that you are well-versed in all developments in the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that quite freely, that I am very familiar with the municipality of Stimlje and the municipality of Urosevac, because I worked in these places. As for the configuration of the terrain, I am quite familiar with it, as well as with inter-ethnic relations in Stimlje and Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you were transferred to work in Urosevac, did all your professional contacts cease with the police station in Stimlje and, generally speaking, with the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: My relations did not cease because I continued to come and visit the police station in Stimlje because it is within the local authority of the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasovic, during your professional career -- well, we can see on the basis of everything you've said so far you've been a professional policeman for 30 years now, since 1975 and it's 2005 now. Were there any complaints from citizens, regardless of whether they were Albanians, Serbs, or anybody else, in view of your professional work, in carrying out your official duties? Were there any complaints? Please, I'm not asking you whether they were justified or unjustified, I'm just asking whether there were any complaints whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: There were no complaints against me, either by ethnic Albanians or ethnic Serbs so far. That can be corroborated by the Ministry of the Interior from Urosevac that is now in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Jasovic, what was the ethnic composition of the employees in the -- in the municipality of Urosevac in the local Secretariat of the Interior? And then could you please explain this to the Court in terms of 1998, 1999, but first generally in terms of the 1990s throughout.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I could not give the exact percentages, but I know that until 1999, until 1999 in the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac, the majority of the employees were Albanians, and they also held the top posts within the secretariat. Also, in 1999 there were about ten employees who were ethnic Albanians who kept their jobs in the secretariat. In this case, I could mention Albanians -- the following Albanians, Avdi Musa and Azem Haliti, who worked in the crime investigation SUP in Urosevac with the department for general crime prevention. Then Destan Sabane who worked on -- who worked in the department for homicide. Then Hebib Koku, who worked as an inspector in terms of felonies in Kacanik. That is also within the local authority of the secretariat in Urosevac. Then Bedri Qerimi, a policeman who worked at the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That will do. Let's just clarify one point, Mr. Jasovic. The few inspectors who are your colleagues, who are inspectors like you are --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- these are Albanians who are inspectors and who worked there all the way up to the end of the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They had the same job as you did until the end of your activities in Kosovo and Metohija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 12th of June, 1999. After that, we left the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All of these police inspectors that you mentioned who were Albanians, they worked there until the very end. Now, tell me, irrespective of those who worked until the end, there were probably others who left the police force in the 1990s. Some Albanians did. This was a widespread thing. And was this something that occurred in Urosevac as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in the autumn of 1990, the majority of Albanian employees in the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac left their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they left their jobs and left the service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues and I, when we talked to them, heard from them that if they stayed at their jobs they would be called traitors of the Albanian people, they would be boycotted by ethnic Albanians throughout the population, and they would jeopardise their own safety and the safety of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to talk to any of these persons yourself, those who were leaving their jobs in the police force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: We talked to virtually all our colleagues from the crime investigation service, and we pleaded with them to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that they left under duress, under pressure that came from their Albanian leaders. Was there a single case in your area, in Urosevac, that anybody was dismissed from the police force or that anybody was treated differently due to the fact that this person was an ethnic Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single employee of our secretariat was not -- not a single one was dismissed or was treated differently because he was an ethnic Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you said earlier that up until 1999 the majority of the employees in the office of the ministry were Albanians, and now you've indicated that others or a large number left in 1990. You say in the autumn of -- the majority of Albanian employees left their jobs. Are these two answers consistent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say here that most Albanians who were employed by our secretariat, in the autumn of 19 -- in the autumn of 1990 left their jobs. Before that, most of the employees at the secretariat had been Albanians, ethnic Albanians. I may have misspoke. I may have referred to the year wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the position in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999, as I mentioned, in the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac there were about ten policemen and other staff members in the SUP of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Out of a total of how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I cannot really answer this question, what the total number of employees was -- or, rather, the exact number of ethnic Albanians in our secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since Mr. Bonomy put this question, perhaps it would be a good thing, perhaps it would be useful, if we would deal with it in greater detail. You indicated a few concrete specific names of your colleagues - inspectors, policemen - who worked in the Urosevac SUP until June 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that, yes. Now, I noted this down. You mentioned an inspector for felonies, Avdi Musa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then also you mentioned Azem Haliti, also an inspector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they work in the same building where you worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: We worked in the same building, on the third floor of the Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The two persons that you mentioned, they worked in the same building where you worked. I'm going to put a question to you later concerning some of the allegations that were made here, that you were involved in extortion, et cetera. So these Albanian inspectors were in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the same building that you were in until you left Kosovo and Metohija in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have to stop now. It's time for the break. Twenty minutes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you said that inspector Avdi Musa was a criminal investigation inspector until you withdrew from Kosovo in June of 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him after you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague Avdi Musa, after our departure from Kosovo and Metohija, from the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, on that same day in front of his house in Urosevac was wounded from a firearm by KLA, and several days later he died in the clinical and hospital centre in Pristina as a result of these serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what happened? He was practically killed. First he was gravely wounded and then died several days later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the other inspector, Haliti, the one that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Azem Haliti, sometime in the second half of July 1999, was abducted by the Albanian terrorists belonging to the KLA from his family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: After one month he was freed. And according to what we know, he is in his house in Urosevac nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come they killed one of them and then freed the other one? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I do have an explanation. Azem Haliti had friends and relatives in the Petrovo village, Racak, Dramljak, Malopoljce, where was the base of the KLA and their headquarters. According to what I learned, he was not killed because that would produce clashes between his relatives and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he was freed as a result of interventions by his relatives.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely as a result of those interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me put a follow-up question. Do you occasionally meet any of the Albanians from Urosevac or from that area since you continued to work in the relocated premises of the SUP Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I continue to be an employee of the SUP Urosevac to this day. As I've told you, this SUP was relocated to Leskovac. As I've already told you, various Albanians come to see us for various administrative issues such as issuance of IDs, passports, and so on. A large number of these Albanians express a wish to see me and to talk to me, and I always accommodate them. When I talked to these Albanians, upon talking to them I learned that terror continues in Kosovo and Metohija carried out by the former KLA members which are now members of ANA, and also the Kosovo Corps, which is the basic force in Kosovo and the secret police. Members of these organisations carry out terror against Albanians, Albanians who used to know and were friendly with the Serbs and wanted to co-exist with them in peace. The Albanians who knew any police officers are also being terrorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jasovic. You mentioned several cases here of policemen who were your colleagues and stayed in their jobs until the end. Do you know whether there were any Albanians employed by the state security service in your municipality? When putting this question, I'm referring to 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me. Until the day we departed, which was the 12th of June, 1999, in the sector of the state security in Urosevac there were inspectors Hisni Topali and Bajram Luri who remained living in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the same Qerimi Bedri familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Qerimi Bedri is a familiar name. This is a policeman employed by the Stimlje police station, employed there, who was sent to work there until we departed Kosovo and Metohija, which was on the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will not put any further questions to you in relation to the Albanians employed in police force. Do you know names of any Albanians who perished because they refused to join the KLA in your territory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know the names of such Albanians. I can tell you here and now that Albanian terrorists, members of the KLA, used terror against Albanians who refused to join the KLA. They also terrorised Albanians who socialised with the Serbs, who had friends among police members, and they also targeted Albanians who worked in state-owned companies and state institutions, as well as Albanians who in any way protested against the violence and terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jasovic. Based on the testimony of the investigating judge Danica Marinkovic as related to the events in Racak, we saw a number of exhibits here of different content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. All right. You're moving on then to the essential purpose of this witness's testimony, I hope.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. But I hope that this is the essential purpose as well, because it is very important to show that the witness had Albanian colleagues working with him at the time of the relevant events, that some of them perished after our forces withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, and as you can see, the witness knows about the treatment that the Albanians who continued working for state organs received or were subjected to at the hands of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the Racak events, when Judge Danica Marinkovic testified we saw a number of exhibits displaying your signature and that of your colleague Momcilo Sparavalo. And would you please tell me, in what capacity did you participate in investigations relating to the Racak events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the events in the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality, or to put it better, after the conflict between the KLA members and members of the SUP Urosevac, at the request of the public prosecutor, in the course of investigation a number of interviews was -- were conducted with ethnic Albanians pertaining to events in Racak and such facts as numbers of the KLA members, their weaponry, their movements, and their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us this: Based on your information, before the events in Racak in the territory covered by your Secretariat of the Interior, how many members of the KLA were in that area, in Racak area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: The territory of Stimlje, including not only the village of Racak but also surrounding villages, were the villages that we covered, because in -- starting in July 1998, until the 15th of January, 1999, when the incident in Racak took place, the members, Albanian members of the KLA, conducted a large number of terrorist acts aimed against Serb civilians and Albanian civilians. Based on the interviews conducted, official notes compiled, and based on the official information, we learned that the KLA staff in the village of Racak was between 80 and 120 members strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jasovic. As inspector of the Urosevac SUP, before the incident on the 15th of January, did you have any intelligence information concerning the KLA, the situation as it existed in Racak and the surrounding area, and about their activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the Racak events, as I have said, based on interviews conducted with ethnic Albanians, we learned that in the Racak village and surrounding -- surrounding villages in our municipality there had been KLA staffs established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jasovic. How did you acquire information about the members of the KLA in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Upon learning about terrorist attacks of the KLA, we as a service intensified our work in uncovering the facts and locating the perpetrators of these acts, as a result of which we conducted a large number of interviews with ethnic Albanians who were able to provide pertinent information to us. I can tell you now that I and my colleagues had informants, registered informants, and also friendly contacts who provided information to us about terrorist attacks, about the strength of the KLA, movement of its members and their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jasovic. You just mentioned informants and contacts you had. When referring to informants, do you actually -- does that imply the contacts that you had among ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among ethnic Albanians exclusively, those who wished on their own to cooperate with the authorities of the Republic of Serbia. And they were the source of this information about the members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, what kind of terrorist attacks took place before the incident in Racak? Do you remember what actually took place and what were the consequences?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's an issue that may be arising, and that is is the witness going to be speaking from intelligence material that he relies on but is not going to be available to the Chamber or to us? We've had this problem before with one of the Russian witnesses, and I recall what the Chamber's general approach was then, but it may be helpful if the accused sets the scene a little more fully before we go on to hear conclusions that the witness draws from intelligence material, if for example, it's going to be claimed that he can speak from such material without it being made available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, find out from the witness if he's going to speak from firsthand experience, if he's going to speak on the basis of information that he received, then find out where that information is from and whether he's able to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jasovic, would you answer the question that was formulated a moment ago by Mr. Robinson; namely, are you speaking firsthand about this knowledge, that the information you got from the people who conveyed this to you, or did you get the information a roundabout way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking firsthand here, based on statements made and given to me by Albanians who came to us on their own initiative to tell us of terrorist attacks, on the basis of statements by individuals who had been taken into custody as well by the police, by the Secretariat of the Interior, and who found themselves to be on the territory of the war or in a suspect place, as well as on the basis of the interviews I had with registered informants and my friendly connections as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So on the basis of all that, all the information you've just presented us with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us briefly, what terrorist attacks were there before the Racak incident in the area itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt again, but I'm not sure we've yet got an answer to the question whether all this material is going to be available to us to consider or if any part of it's going to be subject to an application to say that it can be withheld because it's confidential or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask him. Mr. Jasovic, you indicated you got information from Albanians and Serbs. You had statements --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From Albanians, yes, Albanians. Are you in a position to disclose this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are official reports and information that way contained in the tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean that information is in the bundle of documents about which you'll be testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you'll be able to answer my question. What terrorist attacks were there before the incident in Racak itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: After the formation of the KLA staffs and headquarters in the Stimlje area, in the village of Racak and the surrounding villages, in actual fact, the external KLA terrorists went about setting up fortification. They dug trenches, bunkers and communicating trenches from which fortifications they launched a large number of terrorist attacks on civilians, both Albanians and Serbs, and members of the republican SUP. In June 1999 or, rather, 1998, the Albanian terrorists cut off the main road running from Stimlje to Prizren, and having set up their checkpoints, they began their abductions of civilians and -- of Albanian civilians and Serb civilians. And during that period of time there were many terrorist attacks that were launched against the police, and both Albanians and Serbs, mostly against those people who were running along the roads, and a number of policemen were killed as well as Serbs and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic -- yes. Go ahead. I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember all their names now, but what I can say is this: On the 25th of July, 1998, a policeman by the name of Sladjan Miric was killed. Then on the 31st of July, 1998 again, in that same area a SUP worker in Urosevac, Miroslav Peric, was killed. And two other Urosevac SUP members were wounded on the occasion. Then on the 2nd of August, 1998, a policeman by the name of Boro Stevanovic was killed. In October 1998, another policeman was killed. His name was Ranko Djordjevic. And during that period of time also killed were Albanian civilians Alurin Nazmi, Miftar or, rather, Resani Miftar, Enver Gashi, and I can't give you the other names now, I don't remember then. During that same period of time, on the 27th of June, 1998 in the village of Gornje Godance, the following were kidnapped: Albanian civilians kidnapped from their house. Their name was Suceri Zumberi, and Vesel Ahmeti, as well as Agim Ademi. Then on the 29th of June, 1998, in the centre of the village of Crni Vrh, Stimlje municipality, the Albanian KLA terrorists stopped a bus with Djakovica number plates. They entered the bus, KLA members entered the bus. They were armed with automatic weapons, and they had been trained and wearing camouflage uniforms with KLA insignia, or UCK insignia. And when they entered the bus, they asked whether there were any Serbs in the bus. At that point, they forcibly took off Vojko Bakrac and his son Ivan Bakrac, Genov Stamen, he was an active-duty soldier, and Cuk Djordje was the other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, they were taken off to the Lapusnik prison, the infamous Lapusnik prison. Vojko Bakrac and Ivan Bakrac through the International Red Cross were freed on the 6th of July, 1998, while the destiny of Stamen Genov and Cuk Djordje is unknown. We don't know what happened to them. However, according to some information, they were liquidated, that is to say deprived of their lives at a place called Velika Stena above Gornji Lapusnik in the municipality of Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have enumerated sufficient examples. Tell me this now, please, in view the fact that you were an inspector in the area and the frequency of the attacks, because you've given us various dates dating to the middle of 1998, as far back as 1998, so in view of the frequency of the attacks and the seriousness of the consequences they had, how can you explain why it wasn't earlier attempted to apprehend the terrorists in the Racak area and the surrounding parts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking you, in view of the frequency of these incidents, because you quoted a number of terrorist attacks that had taken place since mid-1998, so in few of their frequency, the frequency of the attacks and the seriousness of the attacks, because a number of people were killed as you yourself have just told us, can you give me an explanation as to why nobody intervened to apprehend the group in Racak before the date of the 15th of January? Why was nothing done about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably they assessed that -- the assessment was that a drive should be launched to apprehend the perpetrators of the crimes of terrorism. However, specifically I can't tell you why. I assume that my superiors would be able to give you a better answer as to why that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Jasovic, in the binder here we have a document or, rather, a number of statements which you and your colleagues collected during your work, your professional work in collecting data and information about the members of the KLA, and before I go on to discuss the individual statements taken by you and others, can we say and can we see that they are very similar in the layout, the form in which they're presented, because the date is always mentioned first, the time, and the name of the person providing the statement. And at the end we can see your signature and the signature of your colleague, Momcilo Sparavalo. Sometimes there is an additional signature, sometimes not. So was this a general formula for taking statements? Was this the standard type of layout and the standard type of statement that you would take as an authorised individual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My colleague and I, my colleague Mr. Momcilo Sparavalo, would take all the statements and they were based on the Law on Criminal Procedure for written statements, and every document -- I can certify every document if the same people took the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That's what I wanted to ask you with the similar appearance of the statements, the layout. Now, let's take a look at the first statement, and the date there is the 22nd of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: What tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The tab is 1.1, 1.1. You've found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is that the statement that you took on the 22nd of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I and my colleague Momcilo Sparavalo took the statement on the 22nd of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, does that statement refer to some information which has to do about the activities of the KLA in the area of Racak and the surrounding parts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was an individual who at his own initiative came to the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac and gave us the names of KLA members, probably from the village of Racak, Petrovo, and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The sentence -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "I hereby state that I own the Petrovo flour mill in Stimlje, where over the past months buyers have been afraid of buying larger quantities of flour from me lest it should be seized by the police. Approximately a month ago, Rama Isuf, son of Hamdija from Racak village came to my mill in Stimlje and said that he could transport flour for me up to Petrovo village with a tractor without any problems. I accepted his proposal and we agreed that for his services I should pay him 100 German marks for every 1.000 kilos of flour transported. I do not know exactly, but I think that Isuf Rama transported 12 tonnes of flour for me with his tractor without any problems in ten trips from Stimlje to Petrovo village. "As I work for money, I sold the flour to decent people as well as to members of the so-called KLA." Now, why did he come to see you, to complain about the police or to make a statement about the KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC
utterances.text: This individual came not to complain about members of the police force but to make a statement about members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
